content:
In France, the social security system ensures that all care related to pregnancy and the period following birth is completely covered at public hospitals. Women who are employed receive 16 weeks of maternity leave, during which they are compensated between €9.29 and €84.90 daily, depending on their prior earnings. When it comes to the financial aspect of having a baby, the situation generally mirrors a family's existing economic circumstances: those who were already in a difficult position remain so, while those who were comfortable continue to be.

However, the picture changes significantly when considering the actual support provided to new mothers. Fathers receive just 11 days of leave, which barely gives mothers enough time to physically recover from delivering a baby. New mothers find themselves juggling the relentless, round-the-clock responsibilities of caring for a newborn while simultaneously trying to heal from the experience of giving birth. On top of this, they face the challenge of finding someone to look after their child, as the options offered through public programs fall short of demand, particularly in and around Paris. The expense of having someone care for a child varies widely. Public daycare facilities can cost lower-income families as little as €1,000 annually, but spots are extremely limited, with only one available for every eight children. As a result, many families turn to private alternatives, including professional childminders or in-home caregivers.
